author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary perfusion pressures.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.description: Introduces the gross structural anatomy of the heart, labeling the four chambers, four valves, and the major vessels that enter and leave the heart.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers of the heart and locate them on a 3D model.
Identify the four heart valves and the chambers or vessels they separate.
Name the major vessels entering and leaving the heart (superior/inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries/veins, aorta).
instructions: Use the Next and Previous buttons to advance through the guided tour.
Walk around the rotating heart model to view each labeled structure from multiple angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Opening clip presenting the slowly rotating heart model and the lab title to orient the student.
clips.narration: Welcome. Before us is a model of the human heart, a muscular pump about the size of a closed fist. Over the next few minutes we'll identify its four chambers, its four valves, and the great vessels that connect it to the rest of the body.

components.text:
FOUR CHAMBERS
Right Atrium
Right Ventricle
Left Atrium
Left Ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Reveals the structure label and highlights the four chambers, focusing attention on chamber anatomy.
clips.narration: The heart has four chambers. The two upper chambers are the right and left atria, which receive blood. The two lower chambers are the right and left ventricles, which pump blood out. The right side handles deoxygenated blood; the left side handles oxygenated blood.

components.text:
FOUR VALVES
Tricuspid (RA -> RV)
Pulmonary (RV -> arteries)
Mitral (LA -> LV)
Aortic (LV -> aorta)

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the label text to describe the four valves, shifting focus from chambers to valves.
clips.narration: Four valves keep blood moving in one direction. The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium and right ventricle. The pulmonary valve guards the exit to the lungs. The mitral, or bicuspid, valve separates the left atrium and left ventricle. The aortic valve guards the exit to the body.

components.text:
GREAT VESSELS
Superior & Inferior Vena Cava
Pulmonary Arteries
Pulmonary Veins
Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Updates the label to list the great vessels, completing the structural overview of the heart's connections.
clips.narration: Finally, the great vessels. The superior and inferior vena cavae return blood from the body to the right atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary veins bring it back to the left atrium. The aorta delivers oxygen-rich blood to the entire body.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: Tracing the Path of Blood
modules.description: Animates a blood-cell marker through the dual-loop circulation, tracing the ordered path through each chamber, valve, and vessel of the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace blood flow through the heart in correct sequence.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit.
Associate each step in the path with the corresponding valve.
instructions: Follow the colored blood marker as it moves through the heart.
Note the color change from blue (deoxygenated) to red (oxygenated) as blood passes the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Positions the blue blood marker at the right atrium and begins the deoxygenated return path of the pulmonary circuit.
clips.narration: We begin the journey with deoxygenated blood returning from the body. It enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cavae. This blood is low in oxygen, shown here in blue.

components.text: 2. Tricuspid -> Right Ventricle -> Pulmonary Valve -> Lungs

clips.changeMeaning: Moves the marker through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle and on to the lungs via the pulmonary valve.
clips.narration: From the right atrium, blood passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle pumps it through the pulmonary valve and into the pulmonary arteries, sending it to the lungs. This is the pulmonary circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: Changes the marker color from blue to red at the lungs to show oxygenation, then returns it to the left atrium.
clips.narration: In the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen, turning bright red. It returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, completing the pulmonary circuit and beginning the systemic one.

components.text: 4. Mitral -> Left Ventricle -> Aortic Valve -> Aorta -> Body

clips.changeMeaning: Drives the red marker through the mitral valve to the left ventricle and out the aortic valve, completing the systemic loop.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood flows through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The powerful left ventricle pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta, distributing oxygen-rich blood to the entire body. The journey then repeats.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3: Why the Left Ventricle is Thicker
modules.description: Compares the right and left ventricular walls side by side to explain the relationship between myocardial wall thickness and the pressure needed to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right.
Relate wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary perfusion pressure.
Connect structure to function in the cardiac muscle.
instructions: Notice how the left ventricular wall is substantially thicker than the right.

clips.changeMeaning: Presents two ventricle cross-sections side by side to set up the structural comparison of wall thickness.
clips.narration: Here we see cross-sections of the right and left ventricles side by side. Notice that the muscular wall, the myocardium, is much thicker on the left than on the right.

components.text:
Right Ventricle
Thin wall - low pressure
Pumps to lungs only

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasizes the thin right ventricular wall and ties it to the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.
clips.narration: The right ventricle only needs to pump blood a short distance to the nearby lungs, against low resistance. So its wall is relatively thin. This is the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.

components.text:
Left Ventricle
Thick wall - high pressure
Pumps to whole body

clips.changeMeaning: Scales up and highlights the left ventricular wall to dramatize its thickness and link it to high systemic pressure.
clips.narration: The left ventricle must drive blood through the entire body, against far greater resistance. To generate that high pressure, its myocardium is two to three times thicker. Structure follows function: more work requires more muscle.
